lesson.title: When to Smile and When Not To: Display Rules for Emotion
lesson.summary: Display rules are culturally learned norms about which emotions are acceptable to show, to whom, and in what situations, layered on top of whatever universal expressive tendencies the face may already have.
lesson.body:
Even if some facial expressions have a partly universal, biological basis, as the previous chapter described, what a person actually shows on their face in everyday life is filtered through a separate set of learned rules. Ekman and Friesen called these display rules: culturally specific norms about when it is appropriate to express a given emotion, how intensely, and in front of whom. Display rules are essentially the emotional-expression subset of the broader category of social norms, the unwritten expectations that guide acceptable behavior within a group.

One of the clearest demonstrations of display rules comes from research reported by Friesen in the early 1970s, comparing Japanese and American participants who watched a stress-inducing film, such as footage of surgery, under two conditions. When participants watched alone, their facial reactions were quite similar across the two cultural groups, consistent with the idea of a shared underlying expressive response. But when an authority figure, such as an experimenter, was present in the room while they watched, Japanese participants were considerably more likely than American participants to mask their negative facial reactions with smiling or a neutral expression. The underlying feeling, as best researchers can infer, was probably similar in both conditions. What differed was the culturally learned rule about displaying negative emotion in front of another person, particularly someone in a position of authority.

Display rules show up constantly in everyday examples once you know to look for them: cultural and gender-based expectations about whether and how openly people cry or express anger, workers in service jobs maintaining a pleasant expression regardless of how they actually feel, the muted composure expected at a funeral versus the open exuberance expected at a celebration, and broad cultural differences in how emotionally expressive people are generally expected to be in public.

Ekman described several distinct strategies people use to follow display rules: masking a felt emotion with a different expression, minimizing an expression's intensity, exaggerating an expression beyond what is actually felt, or simply neutralizing the face to show nothing at all. This distinction between the emotion someone actually feels and the emotion someone displays matters a great deal for how psychologists interpret facial expressions as data, since a face alone cannot be assumed to be a direct readout of inner experience. It also loops back neatly to the facial-feedback hypothesis from earlier in this unit: if someone is following a display rule that requires them to mask sadness with a smile, and facial feedback has any real influence on felt emotion, then the very act of suppressing or performing an expression for social reasons might, in a small way, feed back and shape what they end up feeling.
